Justification 

What makes an action required, permissible, or wrong? Normative ethics asks which reasons justify these judgments. A permissible action is morally allowed. It may also be required; an optional action may be omitted.


Three approaches start from different concerns:

Kant’s deontological ethics asks whether the principle behind an action can be willed as a universal law. His false-promise example tests whether that principle would undermine the practice it relies on. See Groundwork, section II.
Mill’s utilitarianism judges actions by their tendency to promote happiness, counting everyone affected. His account includes differences in the quality of pleasures. See Utilitarianism, chapter II.
Aristotle’s virtue ethics asks what character and judgment enable someone to act well. Habituation matters because repeated actions shape those dispositions. See Nicomachean Ethics, book II.

Harm and benefit to other beings matter in moral deliberation. Whether they settle what we ought to do depends on the account of duties, consequences, and character being defended.
skepticism versus objectivism
These are questions in metaethics⁠: what moral claims mean, what could make them true, and how we could know them.
Moral objectivism holds that at least some moral claims are true independently of people’s approval. Agreement alone would therefore leave their truth unsettled. Moral realism⁠ develops accounts of moral facts, with disagreement about what their independence requires.
Moral skepticism⁠ names several doubts. A skeptic might question our knowledge or justification, or challenge the existence of moral facts themselves. Someone could accept objective moral facts while doubting our access to them, so skepticism and objectivism are not simple opposites.
Further resource: Jeffrey Kaplan.
